title: Buyer beware: Those mummified remains might carry toxic spores
gist: A study in the International Journal of Cultural Property finds that social media has industrialized the trade in mummified human and animal remains, and that sellers ship items showing visible fungal colonization with no safety guidance. The authors argue the real 'mummy's curse' is a biosecurity and heavy-metal exposure risk created by unregulated e-commerce, not folklore — the historical Tutankhamen deaths do not support the curse narrative.

insights.claim: Of 128 public posts offering mummified remains that researchers catalogued, only 24 came from non-Meta platforms, making Facebook and Instagram the dominant marketplace for this trade.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Platform concentration means a single company's enforcement policy is the effective regulator of an entire illicit-goods category — a content-moderation liability vector.

insights.so_what: E-commerce reach converts a niche collector market into a scaled cross-border trade faster than customs and heritage law can adapt.

insights.claim: Mummification has historically relied on heavy metals including arsenic, mercury, and lead, which is why professionals handling such remains wear masks, gloves, and lab coats — precautions no online buyer is advised to take.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Toxic-preservative exposure is a second, distinct hazard from microbial growth, and neither is disclosed at point of sale.

insights.claim: Dormant bacteria, fungi, and yeasts can survive in mummified tissue for centuries and then recolonize and multiply when suboptimal storage supplies favorable conditions and organic material.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The hazard is created after purchase by storage conditions, meaning even a clean specimen can become dangerous in a collector's home.

insights.claim: Sellers provide no safety guidance despite listing items with signs of biodeterioration, which the study's co-author reads as either limited awareness or deliberate disregard of hazards.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A disclosure gap this explicit is the kind of thing that invites platform liability and shipping-policy rewrites.

themes.theme: Documented fungal harm in archaeological settings

insights.claim: Spores of Aspergillus flavus infected and killed 10 of the 12 scientists who first opened the 15th-century royal tomb of Grand Duke Casimir IV Jagiellon in Poland in 1973.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The single hardest data point that tomb fungi can be lethal at scale — it anchors the study's biosecurity case in something other than folklore.

insights.claim: A 2013 study found that the hundreds of mummies displayed at the Capuchin Catacombs in Palermo are prone to microbial and fungal growth after years of unstable environmental conditions.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Even institutionally curated collections degrade without climate control, setting a low bar for what private storage will do.

insights.claim: Scientists identified three fungal genera — Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Stachybotrys — on human remains, coffins, walls, and in the air of crypts at the Church of St. Peter and Paul in Krakow in 2012.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Airborne contamination, not just surface growth, is documented — inhalation risk extends to anyone sharing the room with a specimen.

insights.claim: Of the 58 people present when King Tut's tomb was opened, only eight died within 12 years, and Lady Evelyn Herbert — among the first to enter — lived until 1980, undercutting the curse narrative.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The base rate defeats the anecdote — a reminder that survivorship-style storytelling drives markets for 'cursed' collectibles.
insights.quote: In fact, 58 people were present when King Tut’s tomb was opened, and only eight died within 12 years.

insights.claim: Lord Carnarvon died of blood poisoning from an infected shaving cut on a mosquito bite — technically pneumonia from a streptococcal skin infection per a 1994 Lancet report — and had long been prone to chronic lung infections.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The founding case for the toxic-spore curse has a mundane documented cause, yet keeps resurfacing in media as recently as a 2022 documentary.

insights.claim: Mummified remains are being mailed to buyers nationally and internationally with little or no consideration of health and safety implications, and the study's author calls for clearer shipping guidelines that cannot be misread or gamed.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The proposed intervention targets carriers and shipping policy rather than sellers — watch for carrier policy changes as the first enforcement lever.
insights.quote: There is evidence to show that mummified remains are being mailed to buyers, both nationally and internationally, with little (if any) consideration of the health and safety implications of these actions
